title: Tesla's Missing Autopilot Data Showed It Detected A Hazard Before Fatal Crash, Despite Claims It Was Missing

reading.body:
This is a case about a claim of missing records rather than about the driving system alone. Tesla told a grieving family that the fatal crash data from its Autopilot car was gone, and a hacker later showed that the vehicles retain that data. The failure mode is a party in litigation asserting that evidence does not exist when it does, and the assertion was disproved by an outside examination of the vehicle's own storage.

The disputed material sat in two places in the deployment. One is the onboard data retention in the cars themselves, which the reporting says keeps crash data even when the manufacturer says otherwise. The other is the discovery process in the wrongful death suit, where the family's access to that material depended on the manufacturer's account of what it held. Reporting on the recovered data says it showed the system detected a hazard before the fatal crash. Catching the discrepancy required an independent party to examine the storage directly instead of accepting the company's statement about what was retained.

A jury ordered Tesla to pay more than $240 million, reported elsewhere as $243 million, and a judge later upheld that verdict. What is not established from the material here is the crash circumstances, the court's reasoning, and any question of intent, since the summary supplied is unreadable and the titles alone do not settle those points. A verdict is a finding by a jury, not proof of intent, and the underlying facts of the collision are not set out in what is given.
